_metadata.independence: I read only u16-blind-input.json and consulted no other file, search, web page or API.

hints.reason: Rattlesnake carries SNAKE instantly, but nothing in RATTLE reaches DOG (a baby's rattle is not a dog scene).
Dog bite and snake bite are both everyday phrases, a clean shared verb.

best_available.why: Both 'dog bite' and 'snake bite' are stock phrases; nothing else needed.

pairs.pair_note: BITE is excellent; RATTLE is pure one-sided filler.

hints.reason: Dogs famously pick up ticks; a tick is an eight-legged arachnid, the spider's close cousin, which most players half-know.
Eight legs is the spider's signature and four legs is a dog's; a broad shared property, generic but legitimate.

best_available.why: A concrete dog scene plus a real biological link to spiders; more specific than LEGS.

pairs.pair_note: Both pass but neither is a slam dunk; TICK rewards knowledge, LEGS rewards counting.

hints.reason: Puppies are simply young dogs; there is no recognizable puppies-in-spring scene that a player would reach SPRING from.
Springer spaniel is a fine dog route, but SPRINGER contains the target SPRING as a substring, which is a rule failure.
A spring bounces by definition; a bouncy, excited dog is a real image but far from the first thing BOUNCE suggests.

best_available.why: The only legal hint here; the springy, bouncing dog is a plausible if soft route.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. SPRINGER is disqualified on substring grounds despite being the natural bridge; a replacement such as a leaping or coiled image would be needed.

hints.reason: Lassie is the archetypal famous dog and was a Hollywood movie star, so STAR arrives through the celebrity sense.
Sirius is the brightest star and is nicknamed the Dog Star in Canis Major, a well-known astronomy fact.

best_available.why: The Dog Star nickname ties both words together in a single well-known fact.

pairs.pair_note: Two complementary passes, one via astronomy and one via Hollywood.

hints.reason: Dogs do tricks, and you train a dog to do them; TRAIN is reached as the verb in that shared scene.
Obedience training is the standard compound for dog training, hitting both words at once.

best_available.why: 'Obedience training' names the dog-training scene outright.

pairs.pair_note: Both lean on TRAIN as a verb rather than a locomotive, which is fine under the rubric.

hints.reason: Lab reads as Labrador (or laboratory); Labradors being water retrievers is true but a player sees no water in the word itself.
Paddling happens in water, and the doggy paddle is the familiar swimming stroke that carries DOG.
A dog's water bowl is a single household object naming both words.

best_available.why: The dog's water bowl is the most concrete shared object.

pairs.pair_note: BOWL and PADDLE are solid; LAB depends on breed knowledge the hint does not surface.

hints.reason: A witch's familiar is a well-known trope, but the canonical familiar is a cat; a dog familiar (Faust's black poodle) is niche.
Toto is Dorothy's dog and the Wicked Witch's 'your little dog too' target in The Wizard of Oz, a shared story.

best_available.why: One famous story contains both the dog and the witch.

pairs.pair_note: TOTO is excellent; FAMILIAR is defensible but leans heavily on the witch side.

hints.reason: Wolf pack is the stock phrase and dogs are pack animals that run in packs.
A husky is a dog breed whose wolf-like look is exactly what people know it for.
Both wolves and dogs howl; a shared verb everyone recognizes.

best_available.why: The shared sound is the most immediate link between the two animals.

pairs.pair_note: Three clean passes.

hints.reason: Eggs sit in nests, and dragon nests of eggs are a familiar fantasy image (Game of Thrones, How to Train Your Dragon).
Eggs hatch, and the hatching of dragon eggs is a staple scene in dragon stories.

best_available.why: The verb belongs to eggs and the dragon-hatching scene is iconic.

pairs.pair_note: Both pass; HATCH is the tighter one.

hints.reason: Smaug is the famous Hobbit dragon, and his fire-breathing ('I am fire') is what he does, though FIRE arrives only via the dragon.
Fire breath / dragon's breath is the single defining dragon trait, naming both words.
Dragons spit flame and flame is near-synonymous with fire; reaches both but gives FIRE away almost for free.

best_available.why: Fire breath is the dragon's whole identity in one word.

pairs.pair_note: BREATH is the ideal hint; FLAME passes but is nearly a synonym for FIRE, so it is weak as a puzzle.

hints.reason: Both dragons and fish are covered in scales; a clean shared property.
Koi are fish, and the Chinese legend of the koi that leaps the waterfall to become a dragon is widely known through tattoos and Pokémon.
Magikarp is a Pokémon fish that evolves into the sea-dragon-like Gyarados, but that is fan knowledge and Gyarados is not formally a dragon.

best_available.why: Universal shared property requiring no trivia.

pairs.pair_note: SCALES is strong; KOI is a nice legend route; MAGIKARP is the same idea for a narrower audience.

hints.reason: Haunted is purely a ghost word; dragons do not haunt anything.
Dragons are the legendary creature par excellence, and ghost legends / haunted-house legends are a familiar genre.

best_available.why: Both are creatures of legend; broad but it reaches both.

pairs.pair_note: LEGEND is the only workable hint; HAUNTED is filler.

hints.reason: Blown glass is a familiar craft term and dragons blow fire and smoke; the shared verb carries both.
Stained glass is instant, but nothing about STAINED reaches a dragon without inventing a church-window depiction.

best_available.why: Glass-blowing and fire-blowing share the verb.

pairs.pair_note: BLOWN passes on the verb route; STAINED is one-sided.

hints.reason: Smaug is the dragon who sleeps on a mountain of gold; a single shared image.
Dragons guard treasure and treasure is gold.
A dragon's hoard is the stock phrase and a hoard of gold is what it contains.

best_available.why: 'Dragon's hoard' names the gold pile directly.

pairs.pair_note: All three pass; this is a natural pairing.

hints.reason: Dragons get slain, but SLAIN has no route to HEART.
The 1996 film is a real shared reference, but the hint literally contains both target words.

best_available.why: The only legal hint, though it reaches only the dragon side.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. DRAGONHEART is disqualified by substring; a replacement that evokes the film or a dragon's heart scene without naming either word is needed.

hints.reason: Dragon fruit is a familiar compound, but FRUIT only reaches HONEY via a loose natural-sweetener or honeydew association.
Honey is sweet, but nothing about a dragon is sweet; the dragon-fruit-is-sweet chain is an invented rescue.

best_available.why: Dragon fruit is solid and honey at least sits in the same sweet-food space.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. This pairing lacks a natural bridge; FRUIT is the best of a weak set.

hints.reason: A knight rides a horse and slays a dragon; one figure links both.
You ride a horse, and dragon-riding is a familiar fantasy scene (How to Train Your Dragon, Daenerys).
Dragon and Horse are both signs of the Chinese zodiac.

best_available.why: The knight-on-horse-versus-dragon tableau is universally known.

pairs.pair_note: Three good passes.

hints.reason: Dragon's breath is iconic, and icy breath (visible in cold air, or an ice dragon's breath) is a recognizable image.
Frost is nearly ice itself, while frost dragons are a fantasy-game trope (Skyrim, D&D) not everyone knows.
Game of Thrones is the dragon show, and its source title A Song of Ice and Fire plus the ice dragon give the ICE side.

best_available.why: Breath works for both a fire-dragon and a frozen exhalation.

pairs.pair_note: BREATH and THRONES pass; FROST is close to a synonym of ICE with a gamer-only dragon side.

hints.reason: Iron is forged, but reaching a dragon requires the dragon-fire-forges-steel trope, which is not a common image.
The Iron Throne is Game of Thrones' central object and dragons are that show's signature, a single shared story.

best_available.why: The Iron Throne and its dragon queen live in one story.

pairs.pair_note: THRONE passes via Game of Thrones; FORGE is iron-only unless the player invents a dragon smithy.

hints.reason: Lock and key is instant, but no dragon scene involves a lock.
Dragons guard hoards, but GUARD does not lead to KEY without inventing a guarded key.

best_available.why: Marginally better: a dragon guarding something a key opens is at least an imaginable scene.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. Each hint covers one side only; the pair needs a genuine bridge.

hints.reason: King Arthur is obvious, and his family name Pendragon plus Merlin's dragon prophecies give the dragon side to anyone who knows the legend.
Komodo dragon is a clean compound, but there is no route from KOMODO to KING.
A king sits on a throne, and Game of Thrones is the modern dragon story.

best_available.why: King's throne is universal and the dragon side rides on the best-known dragon franchise.

pairs.pair_note: Two passes; KOMODO is one-sided.

hints.reason: Dragons breathe fire, and you light a fire / fire gives light.
A lantern is a light, and dragon lanterns are a familiar sight at Chinese lantern festivals and New Year parades.

best_available.why: Fire is the dragon's trait and the verb 'light' attaches to it naturally.

pairs.pair_note: Both pass; FIRE is strongest.

hints.reason: Lions and dragons are the two classic heraldic beasts on crests (England's lions, Wales's dragon).
Dragon dance and lion dance are the two Chinese New Year performances.
Lions roar and dragons roar; a shared verb.

best_available.why: The shared sound needs no cultural knowledge.

pairs.pair_note: Three passes with varied routes.

hints.reason: Moon at night is immediate, but dragons have no night association beyond the niche Night Fury.
A lunar eclipse is a moon event, and East Asian myth says a dragon swallows the moon to cause it, but most Western players will not know that.

best_available.why: At least rests on a real dragon myth, unlike NIGHT.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. ECLIPSE is a legitimate but niche legend route; NIGHT is filler.

hints.reason: Mice are tiny; dragons are the opposite, and no shared scene makes TINY point at a dragon.
Mushu is Mulan's dragon, but his being small is not a route to MOUSE; the Disney-mouse link is an invented rescue.

best_available.why: A real dragon reference whose tiny size at least gestures toward mouse-scale.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. The two hints are mirror-image one-siders.

hints.reason: Knights fight dragons, but KNIGHT contains the target NIGHT as a substring (K+NIGHT), a rule failure regardless of the homophone.
Night Fury is Toothless's dragon species in How to Train Your Dragon, a compound naming both words.

best_available.why: 'Night Fury' is the compound and it is a dragon.

pairs.pair_note: FURY passes; KNIGHT is disqualified by substring even though the homophone play is clever.

hints.reason: The leviathan is the biblical sea monster of the ocean, usually depicted as a dragon-like serpent.
Dragons are winged serpents in myth, and the sea serpent is the ocean's monster.

best_available.why: Sea serpent and dragon-as-serpent are both common.

pairs.pair_note: Both pass; SERPENT is broader.

hints.reason: Dragon's hoard is stock, and a pirate's hoard of treasure is a recognizable phrase.
Pirates bury treasure and dragons guard it.

best_available.why: Treasure is the defining object for both figures.

pairs.pair_note: Both pass; TREASURE is the obvious bridge.

hints.reason: Maleficent turns into a dragon in Sleeping Beauty, but she is an evil fairy, not a queen; calling her a queen conflates her with Snow White's Evil Queen.
Daenerys is the Mother of Dragons who styles herself Queen in Game of Thrones.

best_available.why: The dragon queen in one name.

pairs.pair_note: DAENERYS is strong; MALEFICENT's queen side is a factual conflation.

hints.reason: Dragon fire, and Ring of Fire is a familiar compound (the song, the volcano belt).
Smaug is The Hobbit's dragon, and The Hobbit is the book in which Bilbo finds the One Ring, so RING arrives via the shared Tolkien story.

best_available.why: Ring of Fire plus dragon fire is immediate.

pairs.pair_note: FIRE is excellent; SMAUG's ring side depends on Tolkien familiarity.

hints.reason: Dragons have scales; robots do not, and no robot scene involves scales.
Mecha are giant robots in anime, and mecha-dragons exist in games (Mecha Dragon, Mechagodzilla-style), but both halves are genre knowledge.

best_available.why: At least a real genre where robot dragons appear.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. The pair has no mainstream bridge; MECHA works only for anime and game fans.

hints.reason: Mountains are rock, and dragons live under mountains (Smaug's Lonely Mountain) in the standard fantasy picture.
A dragon's cave is its stock lair, and caves are hollows in rock.

best_available.why: Dragon's cave is the stronger lair image.

pairs.pair_note: Both pass.

hints.reason: Roses have thorns; a dragon's spikes are not called thorns and no shared scene exists.
St George slew the dragon, and the red rose is worn on St George's Day as England's flower, but the rose side is English custom few others know.

best_available.why: A genuine dragon reference with a real, if regional, rose link.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS. GEORGE is the only hint reaching both words and it leans British.

hints.reason: Sea salt is a stock compound, and the sea dragon (the real fish and the mythic sea serpent) gives the dragon side.

best_available.why: Sea salt and sea dragon are both established compounds.

pairs.pair_note: Single hint, passes.

hints.reason: Shadow puppets are a familiar art, and the Chinese parade dragon is a giant puppet carried on poles.
Dragon wings are iconic, but WINGS does not lead to SHADOW.

best_available.why: Shadow puppet and dragon puppet both exist as recognizable things.

pairs.pair_note: PUPPET passes on a moderate route; WINGS is one-sided.

hints.reason: Shark fin is instant, but dragons have fins only in sea-dragon or spined-back depictions, a soft reach.
Shark teeth and dragon's teeth are both famous features (and 'dragon's teeth' is a phrase).

best_available.why: Both monsters are known for their teeth.

pairs.pair_note: TEETH is strong; FIN is shark-heavy.

hints.reason: Shelob is Tolkien's giant spider, but sharing a universe with Smaug is not a route from the hint to DRAGON.
Dragons are monsters outright, and giant spiders are stock creature-feature monsters; broad but reaches both.

best_available.why: The only hint touching both words.

pairs.pair_note: MONSTER passes as a broad shared category; SHELOB is one-sided trivia.

hints.reason: DRAGONFLY contains the target DRAGON as a substring, a rule failure; the spring side is also weak.
The Chinese Spring Festival features dragon dances, and the Dragon Boat Festival is a dragon festival; both words share the festival scene.

best_available.why: Spring Festival with its dragon dance covers both words.

pairs.pair_note: FESTIVAL passes; DRAGONFLY is disqualified.

hints.reason: Constellations are made of stars, and Draco the Dragon is one of the classic constellations.
Draco is Latin for dragon (draconic), and Draco is a constellation of stars.

best_available.why: Points at stars directly and at the dragon constellation for anyone who knows Draco.

pairs.pair_note: Both pass on the same astronomy fact from opposite ends.

hints.reason: Hiccup is the hero of How to Train Your Dragon, a title that contains both targets.
Toothless is the dragon in How to Train Your Dragon, reaching both words through the same title.

best_available.why: The dragon character's name makes DRAGON certain and the film title supplies TRAIN.

pairs.pair_note: Both pass via the same franchise; recognizable to anyone who knows the films.
